work.title: Et Folkesagn, Anden Akt
A Folk Tale, Act Two
Ballet i 3 Akter af August Bournonville
Ballet in 3 Three Acts by August Bournonville

history.p: August Bournonville was inspired to write this ballet by reading J.M. Thiele's collection of "Danmarks Folkesagn", published in a second edition in 1843. For unknown reasons Bournonville decided to ask the two most prominent Danish composers at that time: Hartmann and his son-in-law Niels W. Gade to divide the music between them: Gade Acts One and Three and Hartmann Act Two. Nevertheless the music may be regarded as en entity because of common thematic material between the acts. In his diary Bournonville refers to several meetings with the two composers separately but never together. Hartmann is mentioned for the first time on 29 September 1853. "Et Folkesagn" is one of the most beloved ballets of August Bournonville and has been performed 599 times between 1854 and end of season 2014/2015.

titlePage.p: Et Folkesagn / Ballet af A. Bournonville / Musikken af Hartmann / og / Gade.

physDesc.physMedium: Bound in leather half binding with marbled sides. On the spine the monogram of King Frederik IX stamped in gold and: "GADE OG / HARTMANN / ET / FOLKESAGN / PART. / I / 1.-2. AKT. Title page written in Gade's hand. Written in brown ink. Paper: 16 staves. Each act originally paginated separately Act One: 1-74 in Gade's hand; and Act Two: 1-94 in Hartmann's hand. At the bottom of each page a later pagination: 1-176. At the end of Act Two signed and dated: "I:P:E: Hartmann / d: 9. Februar 1854."

annot.p: Act Two on pp. 24-59. Contains Bournonville's notes in pencil describing the mime and choreography in Nos. 9-12 and various other notes in a foreign hands some of them for later revised stagings.

Written in black ink. Paper: 14 staves

annot.p: This fragment was originally part of the 1854 répétiteur's copy (pp. 53-58). It contains the last five bars of No. 12 with Bournonville's choreographic notes and No. 13 ("Troldegalop") in a longer version than the one in the score. (See Knud Arne Jürgensen, p. 169).
